messages.subject: Order of compiler flags
messages.body_plain:
My installation of R on Mac OS comes with default compilation flags like this:

$ R CMD config CFLAGS
-mtune=core2 -g -O2

When I use devtools to load a package, it adds these flags:

> compiler_flags(TRUE)[["PKG_CFLAGS"]]
[1] "-UNDEBUG -Wall -pedantic -g -O0"

But PKG_CFLAGS are placed before CFLAGS, so that the compiler is called like this:

llvm-gcc-4.2 -arch x86_64 -std=gnu99 -I/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/include       -I/usr/local/include   -UNDEBUG -Wall -pedantic -g -O0 -fPIC  -mtune=core2 -g -O2  -c charstep.c -o charstep.o

It seems the later -O2 is overriding the earlier -O0. So when I am using gdb, the library being debugged doesn't correspond 1:1 to the C code, which makes for some confusion.

I can work around this by changing  ~/.R/Makevars, but I'd like to have -O0 when loading via devtools, and normal optimization when doing a vanilla install.packages(), without editing Makevars all the time. Is there a better workaround?

Peter

messages.subject: Re: Non-automatic vignette with devtools?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Will,

I don't think there is a natural way to do this because you don't want
a lot of the standard features of vignettes. Rather than mostly
reinventing the wheel, I'd recommend that you think about how you
could get the most out of the existing vignette system, while getting
as many of the features as you want.  Since you want to use code
externalisation, I'd suggest that you have two external files:

1) run manually, and included with eval = FALSE: that would perform
the computationally expensive work

2) run automatically, in the usual way

If it's possible to split up your work like this, I'd strongly
encourage you to do so.  Otherwise you will be fighting a running
battle with CRAN, who really do want your vignettes to be run
automatically on ever test. Personally, I think that's a reasonable
thing to do - if you want other behaviour you can achieve it using
cached results, or otherwise don't use a vignette.

Hadley

> would like to have a working example of a vignette with these features:

> Is built with knitr instead of Sweave.
> Uses knitr's code externalization feature, where almost all the R code lives
> in a dedicated *.R file. I've added vignettes/CodeBehindVignette.R to
> .Rbuildignore, but I don't know if that's necessary.
> Is not rebuilt every time the package is checked. I am pretending this
> vignette takes a long time to run and compile, and should not be run on CRAN
> or win-builder computer (or even run on the developer's computer is they
> don't want to take 5+ minutes)

> GitHub. Presumably this directory is ./vignettes/FigureRmd, but the location
> doesn't really matter to me. I've added this folder to .Rbuildignore, but
> I'm not sure that's necessary.
>
> I chose an Rmd file instead of a Rnw, so that it could be more portable and
> run on more development boxes, and increase the chance of getting a more
> helpful response. If these two types of files handles things differently,
> I'll add an Rnw example. I am intentionally not using knitr's caching

It's not possible to do with devtools because (by and large) devtools
just provides convenient wrappers around existing R package
functionality. Building every time is very much a property of a
vignette, so fundamentally I think you want something that's not a
vignette (although clearly it's pretty similar). I think asking about
it on this mailing list is fine, although you might get more ideas on
SO.

> It was working exactly the way I wanted before they added the `vignettes/`
> directory.  But I haven't found an example that works with the new file
> structure.  My own attempts didn't work, and even got me scolded.

Yes, I think one of the reasons for the move to the new directory
structure is to prevent exactly what you're trying to do.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: devtools and github dependencies
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Dec 26, 2013 at 2:26 PM, Hadley Wickham <h.wi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Packages would be installed from the first source that had the
> requested version. I think this is relatively simple, and yet allows
> sufficient flexibility. I don't think you want to leave the
> DESCRIPTION file if at all possible.

I personally prefer using URI/URL over a custom syntax; The URL was
designed to solve exactly this problem of locating and identifying
resources, and is widely recognized and implemented. Also you don't
need an intermediate step repository index files (packages.rds, etc).
In the example you give, the package manager somehow needs to figure
out which R packages github user 'hadley' has available, which is not
trivial.

A URL points straight to the source, which is more simple and general.
Because systems like git are also based on the URL, you can directly
refer to any branch for any repo for any user on any server, without
making the system any more complex. This gives more flexibility, and
allows the user to cut out the repository gatekeepers. It would also
make it easier to write alternate package managers that support this
spec; downloading a file from a url is a lot easier than having a set
of predefine repositories (cran, bioc, github, etc), each with their
own indexing formats that need to be queried in order to see what is
available from where and how to get it.

You could still define shorthands for special cases, e.g. extrafont =
github("wch") is short for https://github.com/wch/extrafont/master.

messages.subject: ReferenceClass documentation
messages.body_plain:
A few weeks back, I put together some thoughts about how best to document ReferenceClass (RC) generator objects and their methods <https://gist.github.com/imanuelcostigan/8204819>.

Basically, the real point of contention is how to document RC methods. The official guidance is that they should not be documented in separate Rd files, but rather that (brief?) docstrings could be used. But what if the method requires more extensive documentation? I would love to get some engagement with the ideas that I've put together in the gist, especially now that Hadley's begun to support RC method docs through the github hosted version of roxygen <https://github.com/klutometis/roxygen/issues/168>.

Cheers

messages.subject: Re: ReferenceClass documentation
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, 8 January 2014 08:14:50 UTC+11, Hadley Wickham wrote:
> Hi Imanuel,
>
> Two questions:
>
> * How do you imagine the longer docstrings being included in the Rd files?
>

Only the leading line of the docstring would be included in the RC generator object Rd file (per `promptClass()` output). It seems like the official guidance is that the docstring output is the place to find help on RC methods (as they explicitly state that they should not be documented in Rd files - presumably standalone to the RC generator object Rd file).

> * Why create a new format for docstrings? Why not make them use the
> regular roxygen formatting?
>

The way I see it, roxygen markup is useful for almost everywhere because it allows Rd files to be generated. It is lightweight. But of course, there's a lot that doesn't need to be there if you aren't creating Rd files. Assuming that I am right and that RC methods should not be documented in stand alone Rd files, then you could replace the roxygen markup with something more lightweight like markdown (e.g. instead of @param foo, you could use `foo`, with some indentation). However, if roxygen is processing the first line of the docstring, it might run into some difficulty if you are adoring the first line with markdown syntax that roxygen doesn't like.

So, in summary, RC method documentation would be split between:

1. Docstring that contains fuller documentation
2. Brief explanation of method in the RC generator object Rd file. This could perhaps be the first line of docstring.

> Hadley

I pretty strongly believe if you're going to write more documentation
in the docstring, it should end up in an Rd file _somewhere_, and I
suspect if it's long, it should go in its own Rd file.  But that would

look like - in particularly generating a usage statement that was both
useful and passed R CMD check might be challenging.

messages.subject: Re: devtools and github dependencies
messages.body_plain:
> I personally prefer using URI/URL over a custom syntax; The URL was
> designed to solve exactly this problem of locating and identifying
> resources, and is widely recognized and implemented. Also you don't
> need an intermediate step repository index files (packages.rds, etc).
> In the example you give, the package manager somehow needs to figure
> out which R packages github user 'hadley' has available, which is not
> trivial.

Well just think of those functions as url shortcuts - you could
provide a url if you wanted, but most R packages will come from a
handful of places, so why not capture the most important sources with
some helper functions?  The problem is a little easier than
determining what packages a github user provides, you only need to be
able to determine if they provide a specific package - and you can do
that with a single request.

> A URL points straight to the source, which is more simple and general.
> Because systems like git are also based on the URL, you can directly
> refer to any branch for any repo for any user on any server, without
> making the system any more complex.

But what url would you point to? The url to the page that represents
the branch? The url to the zipball? There's not an unambiguous url
that refers to any git repo + user + branch. And even if there was,
you might also need a url that has the package in a form that's easy
for R to get to. You can't assume that every use will have git
installed.

> This gives more flexibility, and
> allows the user to cut out the repository gatekeepers. It would also
> make it easier to write alternate package managers that support this
> spec; downloading a file from a url is a lot easier than having a set
> of predefine repositories (cran, bioc, github, etc), each with their
> own indexing formats that need to be queried in order to see what is
> available from where and how to get it.

Perhaps you could make that argument if we were starting from scratch,
but we're not, and any new system must be as easy to use as the
existing system for any of the main repos.

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, 9 January 2014 10:06:04 UTC+11, Hadley Wickham wrote:
> >> * How do you imagine the longer docstrings being included in the Rd files?
> >>
> >
> > Only the leading line of the docstring would be included in the RC generator
> > object Rd file (per `promptClass()` output). It seems like the official
> > guidance is that the docstring output is the place to find help on RC
> > methods (as they explicitly state that they should not be documented in Rd
> > files - presumably standalone to the RC generator object Rd file).
>
> What would happen to the other lines?
>
> Regardless of what reference class documentation states, I think the
> vast majority of RC docs need to end up in Rd files. It's ok if
> they're accessible via $help() as well, but most people won't know to
> look there.

The other lines would stay in the docstring and can be extracted using `$help()`.

I am worried about ignoring the official RC guidance at two levels:

1. users will end up confused.
2. the core team will get upset

One mitigating strategy to the second concern (not much you can do about the first) is to refer users to Rd based documentation in the docstring - something along the lines of "See `?RCMethod` for more complete documentation".  I could live with that. But it's still an additional step for the user. As to whether they will know to use `$help()`: that's a good point. However, given the guidance in the ReferenceClass documentation, I would hope that users will figure it out. Package level documentation would clearly indicate that the object is an RC and has certain methods (and possibly even indicate how these might be accessed).

I think duplicating the same docs in docstring and Rd is unnecessary and could lead to conflicting document in certain circumstances.

>
> >> * Why create a new format for docstrings? Why not make them use the
> >> regular roxygen formatting?
> >
> > The way I see it, roxygen markup is useful for almost everywhere because it
> > allows Rd files to be generated. It is lightweight. But of course, there's a
> > lot that doesn't need to be there if you aren't creating Rd files. Assuming
> > that I am right and that RC methods should not be documented in stand alone
> > Rd files, then you could replace the roxygen markup with something more
> > lightweight like markdown (e.g. instead of @param foo, you could use `foo`,
> > with some indentation). However, if roxygen is processing the first line of
> > the docstring, it might run into some difficulty if you are adoring the
> > first line with markdown syntax that roxygen doesn't like.
> >
> > So, in summary, RC method documentation would be split between:
> >
> > 1. Docstring that contains fuller documentation
> > 2. Brief explanation of method in the RC generator object Rd file. This
> > could perhaps be the first line of docstring.
>
> I pretty strongly believe if you're going to write more documentation
> in the docstring, it should end up in an Rd file _somewhere_, and I
> suspect if it's long, it should go in its own Rd file.  But that would
> involve creating some conventions for what a standalone Rd file should
> look like - in particularly generating a usage statement that was both
> useful and passed R CMD check might be challenging.
>

There is something quite zen about docstrings - particularly as it gets rid of the need to process roxygen mark up to get Rd files.

> Hadley
>

messages.body_plain:
Yes, that is a design flaw in CRAN. They should just put the file in their archive right away, and make a symlink or redirect from /src/contrib. A bit more modern/professional archives/repositories, whether it's Github or arxiv.org <http://arxiv.org> or JSS, make an effort to make sure URLs are preserved, because they know the URLS are used to lookup and identify their resources from places that might not easily be updated. (scripts, articles, search engines).

The URL provides a widely-used easy-to-implement syntax for providing a permanent link <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permalink> to a resource. Of course not every website does a good job, as is the case with everything. But the package author can decide to only use URLs from domains owned/managed by a trusted party. E.g. you could just use http://archive.had.co.nz/ggplot2_0.9.3.1.tar.gz.

Hmm, so at least you'd need a note in the doc saying to look at
$help() for more.  That seems backwards to me - I'd think you'd want
the full docs accessible in the regular help, and a basic summary
available interactively.

> I am worried about ignoring the official RC guidance at two levels:
>
> 1. users will end up confused.
> 2. the core team will get upset

My response to this is:

1. Users are already confused. I don't think people even know how to
use S4 documentation and that's been around for years.  Also, you
shouldn't need to know the details of what OO system you're using in
order to get help!

2. There's no point in worrying about that. You can spend a lot of
time avoiding something that you think will upset them, only to upset
them with something else.  With roxygen2, I'll also happy to take all
the heat on any design decisions.

> something along the lines of "See `?RCMethod` for more complete
> documentation".  I could live with that. But it's still an additional step

> point. However, given the guidance in the ReferenceClass documentation, I
> would hope that users will figure it out. Package level documentation would
> clearly indicate that the object is an RC and has certain methods (and
> possibly even indicate how these might be accessed).
>
> I think duplicating the same docs in docstring and Rd is unnecessary and
> could lead to conflicting document in certain circumstances.

But it would never conflict because the Rd is already generated from
the docstring.

>> I pretty strongly believe if you're going to write more documentation
>> in the docstring, it should end up in an Rd file _somewhere_, and I
>> suspect if it's long, it should go in its own Rd file.  But that would
>> involve creating some conventions for what a standalone Rd file should
>> look like - in particularly generating a usage statement that was both
>> useful and passed R CMD check might be challenging.
>
> There is something quite zen about docstrings - particularly as it gets rid
> of the need to process roxygen mark up to get Rd files.

I think that's a stronger argument if you were starting a
documentation system from scratch. While docstrings are definitely a
better approach than Rd files (and maybe better than roxygen comment
blocks), we have to work within the existing ecosystem of tools that
people know how to use.

Hadley

make: llvm-gcc-4.2: No such file or directory

Please install Command Line Tools for XCode (or equivalent).

Or is it always an issue of not having xcode installed?

messages.body_plain:
Some more info on installing cmd line tools, and CC=clang vs CC=llvm-gcc

1. With XCode 5.0.1+/Mavericks, cmd tools are no longer installed. You can do this from the terminal, however:

> xcode-select --install
> softwareupdate -l
> sudo softwareupdate -i -a

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/19066647/xcode-5-0-error-installing-command-line-tools?rq=1

After that, I still don't have an llvm-gcc-4.2. These are the "llvm-g*" applications I see:

> llvm-g++  llvm-gcc

FYI "llvm-gcc --version" says

Apple LLVM version 5.0 (clang-500.2.79) (based on LLVM 3.3svn)

Target: x86_64-apple-darwin13.1.0

Thread model: posix

2. This Hadley endorsed item on Stackoverflow <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/19533220/cannot-install-r-package-from-source-in-mac-osx-maverick> suggests modifying

    /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/etc/Makeconf

changing
CC = llvm-gcc-4.2 -arch x86_64 -std=gnu99
CXX = llvm-g++-4.2 -arch x86_64

to
CC=clang

CXX=clang++

Is that because XCode installs clang by default and llvm is not needed? If so, why is devtools failing on not finding llvm-gcc (and why does it specify 4.2 when Mavericks installs 3.2 by the look of it?

messages.subject: How to help users with install issues?
messages.subject_clean: How to help users with install issues?
messages.body_plain:
A few weeks ago I was thrilled to be able to share my R package with people via github thru the help of devtools.  Now I am in a new position: some people cannot run my examples, and I am not sure how to help them.  For reference:

Here is my project: https://github.com/trulia/choroplethr
Here is my forum for people to report problems: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/choroplethr

The first two issues were resolved by asking people to upgrade their version of R from 2.15 to 3.0.2.  However, now someone has reported an issue with 3.0.2:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/choroplethr/ixFezN2EG8U

I began following up by asking him to clarify what OS he is using since I didn't immediately recognize it.  Once I have that I am planning to try to get a machine with that OS that I can then try to debug locally.

I'm wondering though: is there a standard list of Q&A that people normally run thru when they try to help people remotely with their packages?  I'm basically just making this up as I go along, and was wondering if there is a better way.

Thanks.

Ari
